arakhin-6b-5-5.note: Sha'azrak, an Arab merchant, donated a lamp to Rav Yehuda's synagogue. Rahava put it to a different use, and Rava was angry. Some say Rava changed it and Rahava was angry; others say the attendants of Pumbedita changed it, and both Rahava and Rabba were angry.
arakhin-6b-5-5.why: Rabbi Yohanan has ruled that a gentile's gift to a synagogue may not be put to another use while people still remember him, since he would protest. The Gemara then explains both sides: Sha'azrak seldom came to town, but sometimes he did.

people.name: Sha'azrak
people.about: An Arab merchant who donated a lamp to the synagogue.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage whose synagogue received the lamp.

people.name: Rahava
people.about: In one version changed the lamp's use; in the others was angry it was changed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: In one version was angry at the change; in another made it himself.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: In the third version, angry at the attendants who changed it.

terms.meaning: Communal officials who managed synagogue and charity matters.

arakhin-9b-15-15.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once made nine months of the year 29-day months, yet the new moon still appeared on time. Astonished, he asked how this could be. His son Rabbi Shimon suggested that the previous year was a leap year with a 30-day added month, and two of its months had been lengthened to 30 days. The three short months this year balanced the three long ones last year, putting the moon back in place. Rabbi said to him: Lamp of Israel! So it was.
arakhin-9b-15-15.why: The Gemara is asking how many 30-day months a year may have, and says Rabbi held like Rav Huna that there may be more than usual. This incident is its proof.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who set the calendar that year and was puzzled by the result.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi
people.about: His son, who works out the explanation.

terms.meaning: Jewish months follow the moon and last either 30 days (full) or 29 days (deficient). The court decided which, to keep the calendar in step with the new moon.
A year with a thirteenth month added, to keep the lunar calendar in step with the seasons.

arakhin-10b-10-10.note: The Temple had an ancient reed flute, smooth and thin, from the days of Moses. A king ordered it plated with gold, and its sound lost its sweetness; when the plating was removed, the sound returned. The Temple also had a copper cymbal with a pleasant sound. When it was damaged, the Sages brought craftsmen from Alexandria in Egypt to repair it, but it no longer sounded as sweet; when the repair was removed, the old sound came back.
arakhin-10b-10-10.why: The mishna says the Temple flute was made of reed, not copper, because reed sounds sweeter, and the Gemara has just tied the word for flute to sweetness. This teaching backs that up, and goes on to a mortar with the same fate.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Gemara discusses.

arakhin-10b-11-11.note: The Temple had a copper mortar from the days of Moses, used to blend the spices for the incense. When it was damaged, craftsmen were brought from Alexandria in Egypt to repair it, but afterward it did not blend the spices as well. When the repair was removed, it worked as well as before.
arakhin-10b-11-11.why: This is one of a set of Temple traditions, following the flute and the cymbal, about ancient vessels that worked worse when improved. The teaching goes on to say the mortar and cymbal were left over from the First Temple and could not be properly repaired.

terms.meaning: A blend of spices burned daily in the Temple; the spices had to be ground and mixed precisely.

arakhin-10b-15-15.note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel taught that the Siloam pool once gushed water through an opening the size of a small coin. A king ordered the opening widened so more water would flow, but the flow shrank. When they narrowed it again, the water gushed as before. He tied this to the verse: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the mighty man in his might.
arakhin-10b-15-15.why: The Gemara has been collecting traditions about Temple objects, like the flute, cymbal and mortar, that got worse when people tried to improve them. This one adds a water source, and is followed by more of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's sayings about the Temple.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who teaches this tradition about the Siloam pool.

terms.meaning: A small coin, used here as a measure of the opening's width.

arakhin-11b-5-5.note: Rabbi Yehoshua bar Hananya, a Levite, went to help Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgeda, also a Levite, close the Temple doors. Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgeda said to him: My son, go back, for you are one of the singers, not one of the gatekeepers.
arakhin-11b-5-5.why: Abaye says a Levite singer who serves as a gatekeeper is liable to death, while a baraita calls it only a prohibition. The Gemara first says this incident shows the Sages disagreed, then suggests both agree and differ only on whether a singer may even help.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua bar Hananya
people.about: A Levite of the singers who tried to help close the Temple doors.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgeda
people.about: A Levite gatekeeper who sent him back.

terms.meaning: Members of the tribe of Levi who served in the Temple below the priests; some were assigned as singers, others as gatekeepers, and each group kept to its own task.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Gemara discusses.

arakhin-16a-3-3.note: Rav Dimi, the brother of Rav Safra, fell ill, and Rav Safra came to visit him. Rav Dimi told those present that blessing was coming to him, because he had kept every teaching of the Sages. Rav Safra asked whether he had kept the teaching that a person should never speak about another's goodness in front of others, since praise leads to talk of his faults. Rav Dimi answered that he had never heard that teaching, but had he heard it, he would have kept it.
arakhin-16a-3-3.why: The Gemara has just quoted this warning against praising people in public as Rav Dimi's own teaching. This alternative version says it was not his: it came up in this conversation, where he admitted he had never heard it.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: Rav Safra's brother; while ill, he claims to have kept every teaching of the Sages.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Rav Dimi's brother, who visits him and asks about the teaching on praising others.

arakhin-16b-6-6.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri calls heaven and earth as his witnesses: many times he complained about Akiva to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and Akiva was lashed, that is, punished, because of him. Yet each time Akiva only loved him more. His experience bears out the verse in Proverbs: do not rebuke a scorner lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man and he will love you.
arakhin-16b-6-6.why: Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaria have just doubted that anyone in their generation can accept rebuke, or give it properly. Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri's testimony offers Akiva as a man who took rebuke again and again and loved the one who gave it.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri
people.about: Testifies that he often complained about Akiva to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

people.name: Akiva
people.about: Was punished many times because of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri's complaints, and loved him all the more.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The authority before whom Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri brought his complaints about Akiva.

arakhin-16b-8-8.note: Rav Huna and Ḥiyya bar Rav were sitting before Shmuel when Ḥiyya bar Rav complained: See, Master, Rav Huna is causing me distress. Rav Huna took it upon himself not to do so again. Once Ḥiyya bar Rav had left, Rav Huna told Shmuel what Ḥiyya had done to him. Shmuel asked why he had not said this to Ḥiyya's face, and Rav Huna answered: Heaven forbid that the son of Rav should be humiliated because of me.
arakhin-16b-8-8.why: Rabbi Shimon has just told his son that humility, even when not for its own sake, outranks rebuke for its own sake. The Gemara asks what each looks like, and this incident shows both: Rav Huna's earlier private rebuke, and his yielding only to spare Rav's son shame.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Accused of distressing Ḥiyya bar Rav; he backs down rather than shame him in public.

people.name: Ḥiyya bar Rav
people.about: Rav's son, who complains to Shmuel that Rav Huna is distressing him.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The teacher before whom both men were sitting.

arakhin-19a-3-9.note: The mother of Yirmatya vowed to give the Temple the weight of her daughter. She went up to Jerusalem, had her daughter weighed, and gave her weight in gold.
arakhin-19a-3-9.why: The mishna rules that a vow of one's weight is paid in silver or gold as specified. The Gemara asks whether this incident, where gold was paid without specifying, contradicts that, and answers that a distinguished person pays according to status; she was very wealthy.

people.name: the mother of Yirmatya
people.about: A very wealthy woman, the Gemara says, who vowed her daughter's weight to the Temple.

terms.meaning: The core collection of early rabbinic teachings; the Gemara is the later discussion built around it.
The fund that received money and goods vowed to the Temple in Jerusalem.

arakhin-23a-10-11.note: Moshe bar Atzrei had guaranteed his daughter-in-law's marriage contract, and his son Rav Huna, a Torah scholar, was hard-pressed for money. Abaye asked whether no one would advise Rav Huna to divorce his wife, let her collect her marriage contract from his father the guarantor, and then remarry her. Rava objected that the mishna requires such a husband to vow to have no benefit from her; the Gemara explains that Abaye would have him divorce outside the court. In the end it emerged that Rav Huna was a priest, so he could not have remarried her, and Abaye said: poverty follows the poor.
arakhin-23a-10-11.why: The mishna, citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, makes a divorcing husband vow off benefit from his wife when a guarantor backs her marriage contract, lest the couple collude. Abaye's plan is that very collusion, and the Gemara then asks how Abaye could propose it.

people.name: Moshe bar Atzrei
people.about: Guarantor of his daughter-in-law's marriage contract; Rav Huna's father.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Moshe bar Atzrei's son, a Torah scholar short of money, who turns out to be a priest.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Proposes the divorce-and-remarry plan, then sums up the outcome with a saying about poverty.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Objects to Abaye's plan on the basis of the mishna.

terms.meaning: A husband's written commitment to pay his wife a set sum if he divorces her or dies. A guarantor can promise to pay it if the husband does not.
A descendant of Aaron. Torah law forbids a priest to marry a divorced woman, even his own former wife.

arakhin-28a-10-10.note: A certain man wanted to give away more than a fifth of his property to charity, and his friend would not let him. One version says the friend was Rabbi Yeshevav. Another says Rabbi Yeshevav was the one who wanted to give too much, and the friend who stopped him was Rabbi Akiva.
arakhin-28a-10-10.why: The Gemara has just cited Rabbi Ila's report that the Sages at Usha ruled that no one should give more than a fifth of his money to charity, the view it ties to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya. This incident shows that limit being enforced.

people.name: Rabbi Yeshevav
people.about: In one version, the friend who stopped a man from giving too much charity; in the other, the man who was stopped.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: In the second version, the friend who stopped Rabbi Yeshevav.

arakhin-31a-11-11.note: Rabbi Yehuda reported that Baitos ben Zunin made a conditional sale of his field under the direction of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, and that the buyer ate the field's produce. The Rabbis answered that this proves nothing: in that case it was the seller who ate the produce, not the buyer.
arakhin-31a-11-11.why: A baraita forbids a lender holding a field by conditional sale to eat its produce, since if the loan is repaid that would be interest; Rabbi Yehuda permits it and cites this case. Rabbi Yoḥanan uses the dispute to explain why the mishna calls a walled-city house redemption only like interest.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Cites the case to support his view that the buyer may eat the produce.

people.name: Baitos ben Zunin
people.about: Made a conditional sale of his field.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Directed how Baitos ben Zunin's sale was arranged.

terms.meaning: A borrower sells his field to the lender on condition that the sale takes effect only if the loan is not repaid on time; if it is repaid, the sale is cancelled.
